site_description: Tempo is a free GNOME app to see and manage your systemd user timers: when each one runs next, how its last runs went, its logs, and new timers made from any script, checked before they run.
footer_license: Tempo is free software under the GPL-3.0, made by
home_title: Tempo: see and manage your systemd timers on GNOME
hero_lead: Tempo shows what runs by itself on your computer: when each task runs next, how its last runs went, and why one failed. Drop a script on it to schedule a new one.
hero_soon_text: The first version is being finished. It will be free, with no store and no account.
hero_strip: The last ten runs, then the next
hero_screenshot_alt: Tempo’s home page: the next run in words, then each timer with its schedule, its next run and a strip of its last ten runs
features_title: Everything that runs by itself, at a glance
review_title: Drop a script, get a timer
review_text: Drop a script or a program on the window. Tempo reads it without running it and tells you what could go wrong once nobody is there: a missing interpreter, a file in your Downloads folder, a password prompt, a question waiting for the keyboard. Each problem comes with its fix.
review_alt: Tempo looking at a script: what it is, what may go wrong without anyone there, and the command a timer would run
editor_text: Pick when it runs in words, add conditions (only if a program is not running, only on mains power), and see the next runs before saving. Tempo checks the timer with systemd itself, and can run the command once so you see what it says.
editor_alt: The form of a new timer: name, command, schedule, conditions and the next runs
failed_title: When something fails, you know why
failed_text: A failed run turns the timer red, with the exit code and the last lines of its log, and a notification tells you at once, even when Tempo is closed. One click opens the full log, live, with only the problems if you want.
failed_alt: A timer whose last run failed, with its exit code and the end of its log
system_text: Tempo changes only the timers it created. The others, from your system, your apps or written by hand, are shown with what they do, and the exact command to stop or turn them off if you choose to.
system_alt: A system timer shown read-only, with the commands to stop, disable or mask it
f_logs_text: The log of each timer and of its task, as it is written. Copy it or save it.
f_try_text: Run the command once, after you confirm, and read its answer before scheduling it.
f_safe_text: Deleting a timer can be undone for a few seconds. Pause, resume, turn off and on in one click.
f_keys_text: Close the window and Tempo is gone: your timers keep running, systemd takes care of them.
f_lang_text: In your system’s language, light or dark like the rest of GNOME.
f_local_text: No account and no tracking: Tempo talks to your own systemd, and only asks this site once a day whether a new version exists.
why_text: systemd timers are reliable, but reading them takes several commands and a good memory. Tempo puts them in one window, in words, and makes a new one without writing unit files by hand.
runs_on_text: Written in Rust with GTK 4 and libadwaita: one program of about 5 MB, no Electron, no web view. Tempo does not need to stay open: systemd runs your timers, the window only shows them. For Ubuntu 24.04 and later, Fedora and other distributions with systemd.
install_page_lead: One command installs Tempo in your home folder, with no administrator password. Packages and the source are below.
install_soon_lead: Tempo is not available yet. Here is what it will need.
install_soon_text: The first version is being finished. Its source and an install command will be published here, free, with no store and no account.
requirements_text: Linux with systemd 250 or later, GTK 4.14 and libadwaita 1.5 or later: Ubuntu 24.04, Fedora 40 and later, or any distribution as recent. Tempo manages your own timers (systemctl --user) and never needs the administrator’s password.
source_lead: Three steps, on Ubuntu or Debian (use your distribution’s names for the packages elsewhere).
uninstall_text: The timers you created stay in ~/.config/systemd/user and keep running: delete them in Tempo first if you no longer want them.
docs_lead: What Tempo does, in plain words.
docs_start_1: Open Tempo: the home page lists your timers, with the next one to run at the top.
docs_start_2: To schedule something, drop a script or a program on the window, or press Ctrl+O. Tempo looks at it and says what to fix first.
docs_start_3: Fill the form: when it runs, under which conditions. Check the next runs, try it once if you want, then save.
docs_kinds_text: “Yours” are the timers Tempo created: it can change, pause and delete them. “Personal” ones were written by hand in your own folder; “System” ones come from your distribution or an app, Snap included. Tempo never changes those two kinds: it shows what they do and the commands to stop, turn off or mask them, to copy into a terminal.
docs_actions_text: Run Now starts the task at once. Pause stops the timer until you resume it; Turn Off also keeps it from starting with your session. Delete removes the timer and its task; an Undo button brings them back for a few seconds.
docs_analysis_title: What Tempo looks for in a file
docs_analysis_text: It reads the start of the file, never runs it: whether it is a program or a script, which interpreter it needs and whether that is installed, Windows line endings, whether it can be run, and whether it lives somewhere that may disappear (a temporary folder, Downloads, a removable drive). It also warns about sudo, a question waiting for the keyboard, desktop tools and recursive deletes. Tempo can keep its own copy of the file, so the timer still works if the original moves.
docs_conditions_text: Every few minutes or hours, every day at a time, on given weekdays, or after the computer starts. A timer can wait until a program is not running, until the computer is on mains power, or until a file exists. Options catch up a run missed while the computer was off, spread the start, run at low priority and stop a task that runs too long.
docs_logs_text: Each timer has a log page: what the timer and its task wrote, newest last, updated while it runs. “Problems Only” keeps warnings and errors. Copy or save the log to send it to someone.
key_open: choose a file to make a timer from
docs_trouble_logout: A timer stops when you log out: user timers run while your session is open. To keep them running without a session, run loginctl enable-linger once.
docs_trouble_moved: A timer fails after a file moved: create it again and let Tempo keep a copy of the file.
docs_trouble_edited: Tempo says the files were changed outside Tempo: someone edited them by hand. Saving in Tempo replaces those changes.
docs_trouble_more: Something else? Open an issue on GitHub with what you did and what you saw.
privacy_lead: Tempo asks for nothing and sends nothing about you.
privacy_app_1: No account, no analytics, no tracking, no advertising.
privacy_app_2: Once a day at most, installs made with the install command or from a package ask this site for the latest version number. Nothing about you is sent, and “Check Automatically” in the main menu turns it off. It is the only network request Tempo makes; it talks to systemd and its journal on your computer.
privacy_app_3: A file you choose is read, never sent anywhere, and never run unless you press Try It and confirm.
privacy_site_text: No cookies, no analytics, no third-party content: fonts and images come from this site. Your theme and language choices are kept in your browser only.
not_found_text: This page did not run on time. The links below still do.
docs_notify_text: A timer made by Tempo can tell you when a run fails (“Tell me when it fails” in the form, on by default). systemd itself starts the notification, so Tempo does not need to be open: it says which timer failed and why, and a click opens Tempo. Timers made before this option existed get it when you edit and save them.
hero_install_label: Install on Linux, in your home folder
install_one_text: It downloads the latest release, checks its checksum and installs Tempo in your home folder, with no administrator password. To update, run it again.
packages_text: Each release also has a .deb (Ubuntu, Debian, Mint) and an .rpm (Fedora) for Intel/AMD and ARM, with their checksums (SHA256SUMS). Install one with your system’s tools, for example sudo apt install ./tempo_0.1.0_amd64.deb.
uninstall_source: Built from source, in its folder
docs_updates_text: Once a day, Tempo asks this site whether a newer version exists and says so in a banner, with the way to get it: run the install command again, or download the new package. After an update, the first start offers to show what’s new. Check for Updates and Check Automatically are in the main menu.
